_doc: Where each universe comes from — shown behind the ⓘ button on a destination. One entry per country/universe code in countries.json. `work` is the title, `creator` the author or studio, `year` first publication or release, `medium` the form it first took, `text` a short plain-English note in our own words. Optional `also` lists notable adaptations.

ME.work: The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings
ME.creator: J. R. R. Tolkien
ME.text: An Oxford philologist invented the languages first and the world afterwards, which is why the place names all mean something. Middle-earth is the north-west of a much larger invented history running back thousands of years; the books cover its last few decades before the magic drains out of it. Nearly every fantasy map with mountains in the north and evil in the east is descended from this one.

WES.work: A Song of Ice and Fire
WES.creator: George R. R. Martin
WES.text: A deliberate answer to comfortable fantasy: the seasons last years, the heroes die at the wrong moments, and most of the trouble is caused by ordinary politics rather than dark lords. Martin borrowed heavily from the Wars of the Roses, then added dragons and an ice age creeping down from the north.

SW.creator: George Lucas
SW.text: Space opera assembled out of Kurosawa, Flash Gordon serials and Joseph Campbell's monomyth, set in a galaxy that is deliberately old, dusty and second-hand. The technology is filthy and lived-in, which was the innovation; before this, film spacecraft were clean.

TREK.creator: Gene Roddenberry
TREK.text: A post-scarcity Earth sends explorers out under a rule against interfering with anyone they find, and then spends six decades of television arguing about that rule. Optimistic almost to a fault: humanity has fixed poverty, money and war, and the drama comes from meeting people who haven't.

DUNE.creator: Frank Herbert
DUNE.also: Films by David Lynch (1984) and Denis Villeneuve (2021–2024)
DUNE.text: An ecological thriller wearing the clothes of a feudal space epic. Herbert spent years studying desert ecology and messianic politics, and the book is at heart a warning about following charismatic leaders — a point most readers cheerfully miss. Computers are banned, so everything runs on trained human minds and a spice that only one planet produces.

DISC.creator: Terry Pratchett
DISC.text: A flat world on the backs of four elephants standing on a turtle swimming through space, which started as a parody of fantasy and became one of the sharpest bodies of satire in English. Forty-one novels about policing, journalism, banking, war and belief, all set somewhere with dragons in it.

NAR.creator: C. S. Lewis
NAR.text: A country reachable through a wardrobe, where the animals talk and time runs at its own pace — a year here can be a century there. Lewis wrote it as Christian allegory and also, plainly, because he liked fauns, talking beavers and battles.

HP.creator: J. K. Rowling
HP.text: A hidden magical Britain running in parallel with the ordinary one, organised around a boarding school in Scotland. The structure is school story plus detective plot: each book is a mystery solved by children who should have told a teacher.

WON.work: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland and Through the Looking-Glass
WON.creator: Lewis Carroll
WON.text: An Oxford mathematician's nonsense, invented for a real child on a boat trip. Wonderland runs on logic taken absolutely literally, which is what makes it frightening as well as funny. Public domain, and John Tenniel's original engravings are among the most reproduced illustrations ever made.

OZ.creator: L. Frank Baum
OZ.text: Baum set out to write an American fairy tale without the European moralising, and produced a country of four coloured quadrants around a green capital. He wrote thirteen sequels and never entirely escaped it. The books are public domain; the ruby slippers, being an invention of the film, are not.

GUL.creator: Jonathan Swift
GUL.text: Four voyages to four impossible countries, each one a knife aimed at something in Swift's own England — party politics, scientific vanity, colonial conquest, human nature itself. It survives as a children's story because the first voyage is funny and the rest are rarely printed in full.

VER.creator: Jules Verne
VER.text: Fifty-four novels of geography as adventure, written by a man who researched obsessively and travelled little. Verne's method was to take the science of 1870 and push it exactly one step further, which is why so much of it came true. All public domain, engravings included.

ESEA.creator: Ursula K. Le Guin
ESEA.text: An archipelago where magic works by knowing the true name of a thing, and where the cost of every spell is paid somewhere in the world's balance. Quiet, spare and morally serious; Le Guin also deliberately made her protagonists dark-skinned, and spent decades correcting cover artists about it.

HYB.creator: Robert E. Howard
HYB.text: A pre-history invented to sit between the fall of Atlantis and recorded time, so Howard could write about any culture he liked without a map to answer to. Sword and sorcery begins here: cities are corrupt, wizards are wicked, and the barbarian is the honest one.

CUL.creator: Iain M. Banks
CUL.text: A galactic civilisation with no money, no laws, no work and no death, run by benevolent machine intelligences with silly names. Banks's interest is in what such a society does at its edges — the ethics of interfering with everyone else — because there is no drama available at the centre.

HHG.work: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy
HHG.creator: Douglas Adams
HHG.text: Began as BBC radio, became five novels of increasing bleakness disguised as jokes. The universe is enormous, indifferent and administratively incompetent, and the only sensible response is a towel.

FOUN.creator: Isaac Asimov
FOUN.text: The fall of the Roman Empire replayed across a galaxy, with a mathematician who can predict history in bulk but not in detail. Asimov was 21 when he started it. Almost no action, almost no scenery, and it shaped science fiction anyway.

PAN.creator: James Cameron
PAN.text: A moon whose entire biosphere is one connected network, filmed with performance capture that took a decade to build. The floating mountains were modelled on the sandstone pillars of Zhangjiajie in Hunan, which now has a peak named after the film.

TAM.creator: Bethesda Softworks
TAM.text: A continent of nine provinces documented in obsessive, contradictory in-world detail — thousands of readable books, most of them unreliable. Morrowind, Oblivion and Skyrim each open a different province, and the lore fans argue about is mostly written by fictional historians disagreeing with each other.

HYR.creator: Nintendo
HYR.text: A kingdom rebuilt from scratch in almost every instalment, always with a princess, a sword, a triangle and a boy who doesn't speak. Miyamoto said he was trying to recreate the feeling of exploring the caves and hillsides near his childhood home.

W40K.creator: Games Workshop
W40K.text: A galaxy 38,000 years from now in which humanity's empire is a theocratic, superstitious, decaying horror — and is still the best option available. Started as knowing parody and has been played straight for so long that the parody is now load-bearing.

ME3.creator: BioWare
ME3.text: A trilogy built on the idea that your choices carry across three games, in a galaxy where faster-than-light travel runs on relics nobody built. The politics are unusually good for a shooter: most of the trouble is caused by species who each have entirely reasonable positions.

MRVL.creator: Stan Lee, Jack Kirby and many others
MRVL.text: Superheroes moved out of invented cities and into a recognisable New York with rent problems. Sixty years of continuity, several thousand creators, and a film series that made its imaginary countries — Wakanda, Latveria, Asgard — better known than most real ones.

WHO.creator: Sydney Newman, Verity Lambert and others at the BBC
WHO.text: The longest-running science fiction series on television, kept alive by a plot device that lets the lead actor be replaced entirely. Anywhere and any time is reachable, which is either the format's genius or the reason nothing is ever consistent.

NEV.creator: J. M. Barrie
NEV.text: An island that children dream and then arrive at, where nobody grows older and the consequences are darker than the pantomime suggests. Barrie gave the copyright to Great Ormond Street Hospital, which still benefits from it in the UK.

HAW.creator: A. A. Milne
HAW.text: A small wood based on Ashdown Forest in Sussex, where Milne's son played with his actual toys. Nothing much happens, deliberately. The original books entered the public domain in 2022; the red shirt did not, being Disney's.

GRK.creator: Anonymous, then Homer, Hesiod and the tragedians
GRK.text: Not one work but a contested body of stories, retold with different endings by every city that told them. The geography is half real: Mycenae, Ithaca and Troy can be visited, while the underworld's entrance is a matter of local opinion.

ART.creator: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Chrétien de Troyes, Thomas Malory and others
ART.text: A legendary British king assembled over a thousand years from Welsh poetry, Norman propaganda and French romance. The Round Table, Lancelot and the Grail were all later additions by writers who fancied improving it — a shared universe long before the phrase existed.

ATL.creator: Plato
ATL.text: Invented by Plato as a cautionary example of a powerful state overreaching, and mistaken for history almost immediately afterwards. Every submerged-civilisation story since is a footnote to two unfinished dialogues.

DANT.creator: Dante Alighieri
DANT.text: A guided descent through nine circles of Hell, up the mountain of Purgatory and into the spheres of Heaven, with the poet's political enemies carefully placed at the appropriate depths. The architecture of the Christian afterlife in popular imagination is essentially Dante's invention.

UTO.creator: Thomas More
UTO.text: More coined the word from Greek for 'no place', and it is still argued whether he meant the island as an ideal or a joke — the narrator is named Hythloday, roughly 'expert in nonsense'. Either way, every planned society since has been measured against it.

RING.creator: Larry Niven
RING.text: An artificial band of land encircling a star, with three million times the surface area of Earth. Readers wrote in to point out the ring was dynamically unstable, so Niven wrote a sequel about it falling out of position. It gave engineering-minded science fiction its favourite object.

JP.creator: Michael Crichton
JP.text: A techno-thriller about chaos theory that happens to contain dinosaurs. The film's animatronics and early CGI changed what audiences believed a screen could show, and dragged palaeontology into a decade of public argument about feathers.

PAN2.creator: Suzanne Collins
PAN2.text: A nation built on the ruins of North America, where twelve districts feed one Capitol and are made to send children to fight on television. Collins has said it came from channel-hopping between reality shows and war coverage.

OCE.creator: George Orwell
OCE.text: Britain as a province of a superstate at permanent war, where the past is rewritten daily and the language is being shrunk to make dissent unthinkable. Written on Jura while Orwell was dying; almost every term for surveillance in English now comes from it.

WOT.creator: Robert Jordan
WOT.text: Fourteen enormous volumes of cyclical history in which the same events recur across ages, drawing on Norse, Arthurian and Hindu material. Jordan died before finishing it; Brandon Sanderson completed the last three books from his notes.

ROS.creator: Brandon Sanderson
ROS.text: A world scoured by hurricane-force storms every few days, so the plants retract, the animals are crustaceans and the cities hide in the lee of cliffs. Sanderson builds magic like an engineer builds bridges — with rules, costs and load limits stated up front.

WIT.creator: Andrzej Sapkowski
WIT.text: Slavic folklore rewritten as hard-bitten short fiction, in which the monster-hunter's real problem is always the people who hired him. The Polish books came first by twenty years; the games made it global.

FAE.creator: Ed Greenwood, for Dungeons & Dragons
FAE.text: Greenwood invented it as a boy for his own stories and later sold it to TSR as a shared campaign world. Now the default setting of D&D, the home of Baldur's Gate and Waterdeep, and shaped by tens of thousands of gaming tables improvising on it.

AZE.creator: Blizzard Entertainment
AZE.text: A war between orcs and humans that became a shared world several million people lived in at once. Its zones are designed as sequential tourism — every region is a colour, a climate and a mood you level through.

HDM.creator: Philip Pullman
HDM.text: Parallel worlds where the soul walks alongside you as an animal, deliberately written as an answer to Lewis's Narnia and arguing the other way. The Oxford of the first book is a version of the real one, with airships.

BAR.work: A Princess of Mars and the Barsoom series
BAR.creator: Edgar Rice Burroughs
BAR.text: A dying Mars of dead sea bottoms, flying ships and endless swordfights, written when astronomers still argued about canals. Burroughs's Mars is the ancestor of most planetary adventure; the early books are public domain.

GORM.creator: Mervyn Peake
GORM.text: A castle so vast and so bound by meaningless ritual that it functions as a character. There is no magic in it at all — the strangeness is entirely architectural and psychological. Peake was an illustrator first, and it shows in every sentence.

RED.creator: Brian Jacques
RED.text: An abbey of mice defended against vermin, written originally to be read aloud to children at a school for the blind — which is why the feasts are described in such punishing, glorious detail.

FANT.creator: Michael Ende
FANT.text: A land that is literally made of human imagination and is being eaten by the Nothing as people stop believing in it. Ende hated the 1984 film and sued; the book's second half, which the film omits, is the part about what wishing costs you.

MUSH.creator: Nintendo
MUSH.text: A kingdom of pipes, blocks and cheerful physics whose geography exists purely to be jumped through. No consistent map, no coherent history, and one of the most recognisable places ever designed.

SOL.creator: Stanisław Lem
SOL.text: A planet-wide ocean that is a single intelligence, and a century of human science that has learned nothing about it. Lem's point is that a genuinely alien mind would be unreachable, and that our attempts to understand it would only reflect us back at ourselves.

ORV.creator: Seth MacFarlane
ORV.text: Began as a Star Trek parody and quietly stopped being one, ending up a sincere episodic show about a mid-tier exploratory vessel and the civilisations it blunders into. The jokes stayed; the planets got serious.

SG1.creator: Dean Devlin and Roland Emmerich
SG1.also: SG-1, Atlantis and Universe on television
SG1.text: A ring buried in Egypt turns out to be a door to anywhere, which is a premise built for one planet a week. The galaxy is full of human cultures transplanted from Earth by aliens posing as gods, which is a tidy excuse for filming in British Columbia.

B5.creator: J. Michael Straczynski
B5.text: A five-mile diplomatic station in neutral space, plotted as a single five-year novel before the first episode aired. Less about exploring than about everyone having to live together, which turns out to be harder.

FIRE.creator: Joss Whedon
FIRE.text: One system, terraformed hundreds of times over, with no aliens and no faster-than-light travel. The core worlds are rich and governed; the rim is a frontier, and the crew are on the losing side of a war that already ended.

BSG.creator: Glen A. Larson
BSG.also: Reimagined by Ronald D. Moore in 2003
BSG.text: Twelve colonies destroyed in an afternoon by machines their own people built, leaving a convoy of survivors looking for a planet most of them consider a myth. The 2003 version is the one that hurts.

BEL.creator: J. R. R. Tolkien
BEL.also: Assembled and edited by Christopher Tolkien, published posthumously
BEL.text: The Elder Days, written across sixty years and published four after Tolkien died. Beleriand is the north-west of Middle-earth in the First Age — older, larger and far more violent than the Third Age of the novels — and every acre of it is under the sea by the time a hobbit leaves Bag End.

NUM.creator: J. R. R. Tolkien
NUM.text: Tolkien's Atlantis, which he traced to a recurring dream of a great green wave. Númenor was the reward given to Men for the First Age war, and the Akallabêth is the account of how they threw it away: the one part of the legendarium written as straight political tragedy.

AMAN.creator: J. R. R. Tolkien
AMAN.also: Glimpsed from a distance in The Lord of the Rings, 1954–55
AMAN.text: The Undying Lands are undying because the people living there are, not because a visitor would be. Aman is where the Valar went after Almaren was ruined, and Tolkien keeps it deliberately off-stage — the novels only ever look west towards it, and the one character who describes it is homesick.

EA.creator: J. R. R. Tolkien
EA.text: Tolkien's creation myth, written in a notebook during the First World War and barely altered afterwards. The world is sung into being by angelic powers who then have to live inside their own composition — and the Void outside it is the only place in the legendarium that contains nothing at all.

BR.creator: Ridley Scott
BR.also: Blade Runner 2049, Denis Villeneuve, 2017; from Philip K. Dick's Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, 1968
BR.text: Dick's novel asks what counts as a person; Scott's film answers by building the city around the question and letting the set do the arguing. Between them they decided how screen science fiction looks — rain, neon, advertising and permanent night — and almost every future city since has been quoting the first ten minutes.

FLAT.work: Flatland: A Romance of Many Dimensions
FLAT.creator: Edwin A. Abbott
FLAT.also: Published under the pseudonym A Square
FLAT.text: A Victorian headmaster’s satire on class and gender, disguised as a geometry lesson and now read mostly as the geometry lesson. The Square’s problem is not that a third dimension is hard to imagine — it is that everyone he tries to tell about it is offended.

DIV.creator: Veronica Roth
DIV.text: A Chicago sorted into five virtues, which is either a personality quiz with a body count or a precise account of how institutions recruit teenagers. The trilogy’s real subject is the aptitude test: a system that tells you who you are and then punishes you for being more than one thing.

MAZE.creator: James Dashner
MAZE.text: A locked-room mystery with the room the size of a city and the lock rearranging itself every night. The books are mostly about the ethics of the people running the experiment, who are allowed to be sympathetic — which is exactly what makes them harder to dismiss.

TERM.creator: James Cameron
TERM.text: Cameron rations the future deliberately — a few blue-lit seconds per film, tank treads going over a hill of skulls — and the restraint is why it works. The series is one closed causal loop: the chip that starts Skynet is recovered from the wreckage of the machine sent back to prevent it.

ODY.creator: Stanley Kubrick and Arthur C. Clarke
ODY.also: Clarke’s novel, written alongside it and published after
ODY.text: Film and novel were made simultaneously, which is why the book explains everything the film refuses to. Kubrick got the hardware right by asking engineers rather than illustrators, so the ships still look correct sixty years on — and the most frightening thing aboard is the calm one.

RD.creator: Rob Grant and Doug Naylor
RD.also: Novels from 1989, beginning with Infinity Welcomes Careful Drivers
RD.text: A sitcom set three million years into deep space, in which the last human alive shares a mining ship with a hologram of the bunkmate he could not stand, a creature evolved from his cat, and a service droid with a guilt complex. The science-fiction ideas are consistently better than the budget, and frequently better than the sitcom wrapped around them.
